system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2140-07-07 07:15:00 to 2140-07-10 16:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old woman was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea following consumption of cheese pizza, in the setting of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency. She presented with dehydration and symptoms consistent with fat malabsorption, including greasy, pale stools. Initial management included IV fluids, anti-nausea medication, and a clear liquid diet. Her symptoms improved rapidly, with resolution of vomiting and diarrhea by the next morning. She advanced to a regular diet without complications. Stool studies ruled out infectious causes including C. difficile, Salmonella, and Giardia. Her chronic conditions, including yeast infection, myalgias, and hypertension, were managed supportively. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to avoid fatty foods, continue Creon with meals, and follow up with her primary doctor regarding persistent muscle aches.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
1. Please return to the emergency department or notify MD if you 
experience severe pain not relieved by medication, increased 
swelling, decreased sensation, difficulty with movement, fevers 
>101.5, shaking chills, redness or drainage from the incision 
site, chest pain, shortness of breath or any other concerns.

2. Please follow up with your PCP regarding this admission and 
any new medications and refills.
 
3. Resume your home medications unless otherwise instructed.
 
4. You have been given medications for pain control. Please do 
not operate heavy machinery or drink alcohol when taking these 
medications. As your pain improves, please decrease the amount 
of pain medication. This medication can cause constipation, so 
you should drink plenty of water daily and take a stool softener 
(e.g., colace) as needed to prevent this side effect.

5. You may not drive a car until cleared to do so by your 
surgeon or your primary physician.

6. Please keep your wounds clean. You may get the wound wet or 
take a shower starting 5 days after surgery, but no baths or 
swimming for at least 4 weeks. No dressing is needed if wound 
continues to be non-draining. Any stitches or staples that need 
to be removed will be taken out by a visiting nurse at 2 weeks 
after your surgery.

7. Please call your surgeon's office to schedule or confirm your 
follow-up appointment at 4 weeks.

8. Please DO NOT take any NSAIDs (i.e. celebrex, ibuprofen, 
advil, motrin, etc).
 
9. ANTICOAGULATION: Please continue your lovenox for 3 weeks to 
prevent deep vein thrombosis (blood clots).  After completing 
the lovenox, please take Aspirin 325mg twice daily for an 
additional three weeks.
 
10. WOUND CARE: Please keep your incision clean and dry. It is 
okay to shower after POD#5 but do not take a tub-bath or 
submerge your incision until 4 weeks after surgery. Please place 
a dry sterile dressing on the wound each day if there is 
drainage, otherwise leave it open to air. Check wound regularly 
for signs of infection such as redness or thick yellow drainage. 
Staples will be removed by ___ in 2 weeks. If you are going to 
rehab, the rehab facility can remove the staples at 2 weeks.
 
11. ___ (once at home): Home ___, dressing changes as 
instructed, wound checks, and staple removal at 2 weeks after 
surgery.
 
12. ACTIVITY: Weight bearing as tolerated on the operative leg. 
No strenuous exercise or heavy lifting until follow up 
appointment. Continue to use your CPM machine as directed.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Right TKA, evaluate.

RIGHT KNEE, TWO VIEWS

The patient is status post three-component knee prosthesis in overall anatomic
alignment.  No fracture detected.  There is probable joint effusion, soft
tissue edema, subcutaneous emphysema, skin staples and drain, all compatible
with recent surgery.

diagnoses.long_title: Osteoarthrosis, localized, not specified whether primary or secondary, lower leg
Personal history of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the orthopedic team. You're here today for your right knee replacement, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been in so much pain for months. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Osteoarthritis can really limit your mobility. The surgery is scheduled for later today, and Dr. Patel will be performing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little nervous. I’ve had infections before—MRSA in my leg. Is that going to be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important to know, and we’ve noted it. You’ll get IV antibiotics before and for 24 hours after surgery to lower that risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. What about my other medicines? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your list. You’re on metoprolol for blood pressure, Creon for your pancreas, B12 shots, and Mirapex for restless legs. We’ll restart most after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma? I have my inhaler.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can use your albuterol as needed. We’ll keep it at your bedside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also have depression and PTSD. Sometimes I get anxious in hospitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of that. The team will check in regularly. If you feel overwhelmed, just let us know. We can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from surgery. Everything went smoothly. You have a drain and a dressing, and your pain is being managed with a PCA pump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy. Is the knee okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the implant is in good alignment. You’ll get a report later, but initial signs are excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your X-ray shows the prosthesis is well-placed. There’s some swelling and fluid, but that’s expected after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that go down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, over the next few days. We’ll keep an eye on it and manage swelling with elevation and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still sore. I’m off the PCA now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve switched to oral pain meds—oxycodone as needed. We’ll keep it controlled while avoiding heavy sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also feeling a bit weak. Did I lose blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hematocrit dropped to 27, and your blood pressure was low, so we gave you one unit of blood yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t know that. Am I stable now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your latest hematocrit is 32.6, and your vitals are stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my iron? I can’t take supplements—they make me sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. For now, we’re focusing on recovery. Your B12 and diet will help. We’ll discuss long-term options later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The drain and Foley catheter were removed this morning. You did well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I start moving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy will see you today. You can bear weight as tolerated. We’ll also start the CPM machine to help with motion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: CPM machine? What does that do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It gently bends and straightens your knee to prevent stiffness. We’ll start slow and increase as you tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The therapist was here. It was tiring, but I did it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job. Progress takes time. Keep drinking fluids and eating well to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve prescribed docusate and senna to help. Drink plenty of water and let us know if it’s a problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We removed the dressing today. Your incision looks clean, dry, and healing well—no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You can shower five days after surgery—so day 5. No baths or soaking for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A visiting nurse will remove them in two weeks. Keep an eye out for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on lovenox for blood clot prevention. It’s a daily injection for three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had DVT before. Is this to prevent another?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. After knee surgery, the risk is higher. After the injections, you’ll switch to aspirin for three more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re doing well—pain controlled, eating normally, and your wound looks great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home, but nervous about managing alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have home health services—nursing for wound checks and PT visits. Staples will be removed in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Should I restart everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your home medications except NSAIDs—no ibuprofen or advil. They can interfere with healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In four weeks. Call to confirm the appointment. If you have fever, increased pain, or redness, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t drive, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not until cleared by your surgeon. Use your CPM machine at home as directed, and keep moving safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m hopeful this will help me walk better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident it will. You’ve made great progress. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old woman was admitted for elective right total knee arthroplasty due to severe osteoarthritis. She has a complex medical history including chronic pancreatitis, hypertension, depression, PTSD, restless legs syndrome, asthma, venous insufficiency, and a history of MRSA infections and DVT. The surgery was performed successfully on the day of admission. Postoperatively, she received IV antibiotics and lovenox for prophylaxis, was transitioned from PCA to oral pain control, and began physical therapy with weight-bearing as tolerated and CPM machine use. She required one unit of blood on postoperative day one due to anemia from a hematocrit of 27. Her recovery was uncomplicated, with stable vital signs, adequate pain control, and a clean, healing incision. She was discharged home with home health services, instructions for wound care, anticoagulation with lovenox followed by aspirin, and a follow-up appointment in four weeks.
